name: Program Evaluation
title: Program Evaluation
answer: Program evaluation is the practice of checking whether a program or tool actually produced the gains it promised, by comparing students who used it with similar students who did not. It matters because districts spend money on programs and need to know what works, and because honest findings, including disappointing ones, free up money and time for better options.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Program evaluation applies the pilot method to every program a district buys or runs, so that spending is judged by results rather than by vendor claims. The strongest evaluations compare students who used the program with similar students who did not, because without a comparison a district cannot tell whether any gains came from the program or from something else. It also covers intervention results tracking, which shows whether students receiving extra help are catching up. Multi tiered systems of support platforms can follow each student's progress through interventions, and AI can help teams see which interventions are working for which students. The point is to give teams the information they need to decide whether to continue, change, or end an intervention.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, evaluation starts with a comparison group rather than a single group measured before and after. Intervention results tracking sits alongside it, with multi tiered systems of support platforms recording each student's progress through the interventions they receive, and AI helping teams spot which interventions work for which students. The team then decides whether to continue, change, or end an intervention based on what the tracking shows. The text does not give grade band examples for this idea. Findings are shared honestly, including disappointing ones, because a program that did not work is valuable information that frees money and time for something better.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with evidence from a meta analysis of AI in K through 12 math, which found a small positive effect of about 0.34 standard deviations, larger for tutoring and adaptive systems (Yi et al., 2024). It notes that most education programs that work produce effects in a similar range, so expectations should be realistic. A vendor promising dramatic gains should be asked for evidence. The text also states that districts that report only successes lose credibility, and that boards and families deserve the full picture.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by the comparison requirement: without a comparison group, a district cannot tell whether gains came from the program or from something else, so evaluation claims are weak without one. Expectations should stay realistic, since most programs that work produce effects in a similar range, and a vendor promising dramatic gains should be asked for evidence. The decision to continue, change, or end an intervention stays with the team, not with the platform or the AI. Evaluation findings should be shared honestly, including disappointing ones, because districts that report only successes lose credibility and boards and families deserve the full picture.
